title: Dissociable neurocognitive mechanisms of state and trait anxiety in working memory: Threat-induced alterations in decision dynamics and attenuation of large-scale network reconfiguration
abstract: Trait and state anxiety represent dissociable dimensions that influence working memory (WM) through distinct neurocognitive mechanisms. However, how each dimension modulates WM performance and large-scale brain network interactions under threat remains poorly understood. This study disentangled their respective contributions by integrating an interference-suppression WM task with a threat-of-shock paradigm, complemented by hierarchical drift-diffusion modeling (HDDM) and functional network connectivity (FNC) analyses. Threat-induced state anxiety robustly accelerated reaction times across all task conditions, whereas trait anxiety exerted a selective effect, impairing accuracy specifically in the highest-interference condition. HDDM revealed that state anxiety was associated with reduced decision threshold, shortened non-decision time, and task-dependent increases in drift rate. This pattern of effects is consistent with an urgency-driven shift in decision policy toward faster, less cautious responding. FNC analyses indicated that state anxiety attenuated task-evoked network reconfiguration, weakening segregation between the anterior default network (aDN) and task-positive networks (dorsal attention network, frontoparietal control network [FPCN]), while also reducing aDN-posterior default network coupling. Resting-state analyses identified heightened aDN-FPCN anticorrelation as a stable neural correlate of trait anxiety, and this anticorrelation was selectively associated with trait worry in the High Trait Anxiety group. These findings reveal a dissociation: state anxiety drives context-dependent shifts in decision policy and task-evoked network reconfiguration, while trait anxiety manifests primarily as a stable intrinsic network characteristic with selective behavioral expression under low-to-moderate cognitive load.

title: [The research progress and outlook on the effects of different exercise modalities on working memory function in middle-aged and elderly individuals].
abstract: This review provides a comprehensive analysis of the effects of different exercise modalities on working memory function in middle-aged and older adults. It systematically reviews evidence from interventions including aerobic exercise, resistance training, and traditional mind-body exercises, examining their acute effects and long-term mechanisms of action. The findings indicate that aerobic exercise enhances working memory by improving cerebral blood flow, promoting neuroplasticity, and upregulating brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) levels. Resistance training activates neuroadaptive remodeling mechanisms and optimizes cerebral hemodynamics, thereby strengthening executive control. Traditional mind-body exercises improve the efficiency of cognitive control networks by restructuring functional neural networks and modulating the stress-inflammation axis. Combined exercise regimens, which integrate the synergistic effects of aerobic and resistance training, can further improve working memory performance. Mechanistic studies indicate that exercise interventions optimize neural network function through multiple pathways, including BDNF-mediated synaptic plasticity enhancement, coordinated regulation of the dopaminergic/noradrenergic systems, and improvements in cerebral blood flow and vascular reactivity. A dynamic individualized prescription design based on physiological and cognitive baseline characteristics may maximize cognitive health benefits. Future research should integrate multimodal neuroimaging technologies to clarify the neural mechanisms underlying exercise interventions and develop artificial intelligence-driven personalized prescription systems. At the policy level, integrating sports and medical services and promoting the large-scale application of exercise interventions in populations with multimorbidity are critical to addressing the public health challenges associated with population aging.

title: Predicting visual working memory errors with a priori measures of representational geometry from human and artificial systems
abstract: A longstanding question in cognitive science is whether the structure of mental representations — deriving from perceptual and semantic knowledge — can be used to generate a priori quantitative predictions of the specific errors people make in memory. Using both human similarity judgments and an ensemble of modern pretrained deep neural networks trained for general visual tasks, with no memory-task or face-identification training, we measure the representational geometry of face stimuli and simple visual features (e.g., color, shape, orientation, location) independently of any memory experiment. Combined with a simple single-parameter decision rule, these independently measured geometries predict the full distribution of visual working memory errors for those stimuli, including which specific items people are most likely to confuse, without any fitting to the memory data. Human and deep network-derived geometries agree closely, and together they outperform standard mixture model and tuning-function models of memory while using fewer free parameters. The same pipeline, with a fixed modeling procedure, transferred unchanged to thirty new face sets as well as novel tasks and simple stimuli like orientation, shape, color and location, in each case predicting the specific pattern of errors specifically from that set’s unique network-derived geometry. Because the same geometric measurement underlies predictions across different aspects of behavior, the results suggest that representational geometry, measured with modern tools, provides a direct and falsifiable a priori link between internal representations and the errors people make in memory.

title: Development of Working Memory Across Toddlerhood and Implications for Language Development: Integrating Neuroimaging and Visual-Attentional Evidence
abstract: Many aspects of cognitive growth hinge on children’s developing working memory (WM henceforth) and language skills (Passolunghi & Siegel, 2001; Vernucci et al., 2020; Lany, 2017). For instance, toddlers with a stronger WM tend to process transient speech more efficiently (Ronfard, Wei, & Rowe, 2021). However, studies examining the link between WM and language development have predominantly focused on older children, due in part to a lack of infant- and toddler-friendly tasks that sensitively detect individual differences in emerging WM. Even less is known about the neural correlates of WM during toddlerhood and their relations with early vocabulary and syntactic growth. In the current study, we measured children’s WM using event-related potential (ERP) and eye tracking indices and aim to 1) chart the developmental advances in WM during toddlerhood and 2) investigate whether individual differences in WM relate to variation in children’s language skills. The findings may shed light on the developmental advances in WM across toddlerhood and the neural networks and visual-attentional processes underlying WM growth. Moreover, understanding the associations between ERP/eye tracking measures and language skills may provide new insights into the cognitive resources and neural architecture contributing to early lexical and syntactic development.

title: Intrinsic Functional Architecture Reflects Individual Differences in Passive Working Memory: An Exploratory Resting‐State fMRI Study
abstract: Passive working memory (WM) is rarely detectable because it is thought to rely less on persistent neural firing, leaving a minimal trace in ongoing brain activity. This elusive nature poses a major challenge for exploring its neural basis. While the activity-silent working memory (ASWM) framework proposes that such latent representations are maintained through transient reconfiguration in intrinsic functional connectivity, tracking these rapid dynamics via functional MRI remains methodologically difficult. Alternatively, investigating the brain's intrinsic functional architecture provides insights into the baseline "neural scaffolding" that predisposes individuals to successful passive WM. To explore this, we combined pre-task resting-state fMRI, structural MRI, and behavioral data from a sequential change-detection paradigm in 151 healthy adults. Functional connectivity-behavior associations revealed that individual differences in passive WM performance were significantly reflected by intrinsic connections among large-scale networks encompassing dorsal attention, control, and sensorimotor. Granger causality analyses further revealed a group-level temporal dependency pattern linking these functional systems. Furthermore, exploratory structural analyses suggested spatial convergence between uncorrected cortical-thickness associations and certain functionally identified sensorimotor nodes. Overall, this study adopts an exploratory approach to demonstrate that baseline intrinsic functional architecture-complemented by preliminary structural findings-is significantly associated with individual differences in passive WM.

title: Table 1_Working memory network dysfunction in bipolar I vs. bipolar II disorder: a systematic review of task-fMRI evidence.docx
abstract: Background Working memory impairment is one of the core cognitive phenotypes in bipolar disorder. However, whether the task-based functional magnetic resonance imaging mechanisms underlying working memory processing are consistent between bipolar disorder type I (BD-I) and type II (BD-II) remains unclear. This systematic review summarizes task-based fMRI evidence, with a focus on characterizing the neural correlates of working memory in BD-II and comparing them with BD-I. Methods Following the PRISMA 2020 guidelines, PubMed, Embase, and Web of Science were systematically searched for studies published between January 2011 and June 2025. Eligible studies included task-based fMRI investigations in adults using working memory paradigms that separately reported results for BD-I and BD-II. A total of 22 studies were included for qualitative synthesis. Results Across 22 task-based fMRI studies, the qualitative evidence suggests potentially different patterns of working-memory network engagement in BD-I and BD-II; however, subtype-specific inference is constrained by the very limited BD-II literature, with only three studies including BD-II samples (one BD-II-only study and two direct BD-I vs BD-II comparisons). In BD-I, studies more often reported altered or less efficient recruitment of executive-control regions/networks and reduced task-related suppression of default-mode regions under higher cognitive load and/or emotional distraction. In BD-II (based on sparse evidence), euthymic samples were generally reported to show relatively preserved recruitment and performance, whereas depressive-state or higher-demand conditions were associated with attenuated load-related upregulation. In a single emotional-interference paradigm, BD-II showed stronger inverse DLPFC–amygdala coupling, which may reflect context-specific modulation of fronto-limbic interactions. Conclusion The current task-fMRI literature provides preliminary, hypothesis-generating indications that BD-I and BD-II may not be fully captured by a simple severity-continuum account, but firm subtype-specific conclusions are not yet warranted given the scarcity of BD-II studies and the limited number of direct BD-I/BD-II comparisons. Across studies, BD-I findings have more often been interpreted within neural inefficiency/limited-scalability accounts and reduced task-related DMN suppression, whereas BD-II findings—based on sparse evidence—have been reported as more state- and context-dependent. Larger, harmonized studies with direct BD-I/BD-II comparisons and mood-state stratification are needed to test these provisional patterns.

title: Effects of Children's Video Gaming Experience on Chinese Orthographic Processing and Its Neural Mechanisms
abstract: This study investigates the effects of gaming genres on behavioral and neural mechanisms of Chinese orthographic processing. A total of 1462 primary school students completed a gaming and reading experience questionnaire and an orthographic judgment task, with 45 participants undergoing fMRI scans during orthographic and font size judgment tasks. Participants were categorized into three groups: action video gamers, non-action video gamers, and non-video gamers. Behavioral analyses revealed that action video gamers outperformed the other groups in orthographic skills, when age, gender, and video gaming time were statistically controlled. Neural analyses focused on modular interactions among vision, attention, and working memory networks. During the orthographic judgment task, action video gamers exhibited significantly stronger vision-working memory modular interaction compared to the other groups. No significant group differences were observed in vision-attention modular interactions during the orthographic judgment task or in any modular interaction during the font size judgment task, suggesting cognition-specific and task-specific effects. These findings highlight the potential benefits of action video gaming on orthographic processing and its associated neural networks, particularly in integrating vision and working memory. SUMMARY: Action video gamers outperformed others in orthographic processing skills. Action video gaming was associated with better vision-working memory neural interactions. Modular interactions were cognition-specific and task-specific.

title: Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation combined with Tai Chi improves working memory in older adults with sleep disorders and mild cognitive impairment: An fMRI-based randomized controlled trial
abstract: BACKGROUND: Working memory impairment has been reported in older adults with sleep disorders and MCI, with the frontoparietal network playing a central role in working memory. The key question is whether integrating Tai Chi with rTMS improves working memory, and whether such improvements result from the modulation of frontoparietal networks plasticity. METHODS: Seventy-one participants with sleep disorders and MCI were assigned to the experimental group (Tai Chi + 1-Hz rTMS, n = 37) or sham group (Tai Chi + sham rTMS, n = 34). They completed 6 weeks of Tai Chi combined with neuronavigated rTMS targeted the right DLPFC and underwent fMRI scans. Outcomes included Numerical N-back task, digit span task，Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA). Task fMRI measured N-back activation patterns, and seed-based resting-state functional connectivity (rsFC) was assessed. Correlations between the activation/rsFC and N-back task performance were explored. RESULTS: Seventy-one participants (mean age 67.6 ± 4.6 years; 30 male [42%], 41 female [58%]) were included. After 6 weeks, the experimental group showed significant improvements versus shams in PSQI, MoCA, 0-back and 2-back task accuracy, 0-back reaction time, and forward digit span (all p < 0.05). The 2-back accuracy was negatively correlated with right precuneus activation (r = -0.381, p = 0.034) and positively correlated with right precuneus connectivity to the left SMA (r = 0.367, p = 0.042). CONCLUSION: Adjunctive neuronavigated rTMS delivered in addition to Tai Chi training may enhance working memory rehabilitation in older adults with sleep disorders and MCI, with frontoparietal network modulation as a potential neural basis. TRIAL REGISTRATION: Clinical trial registration no. ChiCTR 2200063274.

title: Two Logics of Memory
abstract: Introduction The concepts of “digital afterlife” and “digital legacy” are currently spreading across the Internet, signalling an emerging industry fuelled by artificial intelligence (AI) focussed on grief and loss. “Griefbots”, “deadbots”, and “digital twins”, derivatives of the increasingly widespread companion AI (Malfacini), offer replicas of deceased people by enmeshing generative artificial intelligence (Large Language Models of Transformer architecture) and surveillance-level data collection. The self-defined “grief tech” offers to keep alive the memory of those who have passed through the creation of digital representations with conversational interfaces with which the user can indefinitely talk, mimicking appearance and behaviour through the use of gathered online data—such as voice and video recordings, biometrics, photographs, emails and social media interactions. These products ultimately offer a restoration of presence before loss and the mitigation of grief through digital performance. We argue that underpinning these AI grief technologies is an understanding of what memory is that operates through a conflation of computational processes and human memory. Furthermore, we contend that this equation of memory with a set of computational procedures of high complexity underlies the commodification of human interior life within an expanding political economy that seeks to mine and capitalise on emotional resources through technology; an operation embedded in the rapid integration of AI as a new medium, which ultimately works against the human faculty of memory as an essential (re)constitutive narrative process of the self. The Underlying Conflation of Memory and Computation Several startups have emerged during the past years offering digital products based on providing simulations of deceased people. The names of these companies already advance absolute claims: Replika is directly named after the concept of a replica of a person; You, Only Virtual speaks directly to a possibility of retaining selfhood in a split version; HereAfterAI obliquely names death itself. Their marketing pitches offer to help the bereaved to remember their loved ones, granting a remedy to forgetfulness—HereAfterAI, for example, promises to “reinvent remembering”, while You, Only Virtual claims to “transform how the world experiences grief and remembrance”. Bolder versions of these products offer straightforward communication with the deceased: You, Only Virtual offers on its front page “AI-powered communication with those we’ve lost”; similarly, Seance grants to “let your loved ones speak to your heart once again”. A long-standing science fiction trope underlies these marketing promises: the imaginary of uploading, downloading, and retrieving consciousness from its physical embodiment in a person to an external device that can contain what ultimately constitutes the self. The dystopian 2019 series Years and Years depicts a near future in which a person’s mind is uploaded onto a server, to be retrieved by subsequent generations as though consulting an interactive digital archive in a largely disembodied world in which we all interact as holograms—therefore allowing for the complete indifferentiation between actual (disembodied) people and those who no longer live but have had their minds uploaded. The 2021 series Solos moves the premise further and closer to the present: a man, terminally ill, purchases an identical fleshed-out replica of himself, designed to replace him as a father to his children after his death. The man tests and confirms that his replica thinks and feels—and would react in future hypothetical scenarios he has not yet lived—exactly as he would. As Carl Freedman argues, what is distinctive to the science fiction genre is that it keeps a rationally accountable link, by means of which its premise never falls onto fantasy ground but stays in the realm of reality, managing to stay within its parameters through explanations provided by—fictional—science. In the Solos episode, the replica is able to come up with its own spontaneous reasoning—not executing mere archival retrieval, but generative responses. Generative AI systems’ ability to produce seemingly original content from what the Internet’s archive has given them, largely due to their extraordinarily plastic use of language, has already grounded that imaginary link. The recently popularised notion of “neural networks” takes that further, as it circulates beyond the AI study field, advancing imaginaries of the replication of the brain’s functioning, whereby the ability to recreate neurons would imply the ability to recreate the way a brain works. In all these accounts of extended presence through synthetic forms of conservation of the self, an interplay is put into motion between replication and actual identity of the replicated being. Whether retained as a form of soul or consciousness in an external device (as depicted in Years and Years) or replicated as a simulation that manages to bring up the actual person by means of sheer algorithmic performance (as in the Solos episode), a core conceptualisation of selfhood is at stake. Insofar as these depictions foster the premise that someone can be replicated through a management of their gathered data, it incites an idea of self and personhood that can in some way be eventually equated to a sum of data; a notion which can ultimately be traced back to the computational model of memory. Two Logics of Memory The longstanding brain as computer metaphor, whose scientific roots lie in mid-twentieth-century cybernetics and cognitive science as advanced by cybernetics founders Norbert Wiener and John von Neumann (Hayles), migrated from metaphorical expressions stemming from the computational sciences into everyday language as an uncontested analogy whose figurative nature is often overlooked (Innocenti). As scholars have persistently pointed out throughout the past decades (Carbonell et al.; Colburn and Shute; Möck), in technology, particularly, the metaphors designed to circulate complex and abstract concepts usually have a bidirectional impact, ultimately shaping the very research questions that inform objects, concepts and entire fields of study (Gozzi). On this basis, the above-mentioned imaginaries of fiction as well as the grief-oriented companies’ marketing rhetoric resort to a conflating conceptualisation of memory stemming from the brain as a computer/computer as a brain metaphor: human memory is equated to a computer’s technical capacity for storage and retrieval of information, whether as working memory actively processed during operation or as long-term storage written to disk. Yet the differences are vast and substantial. Computational memory is the technical capacity of digital systems to store, retrieve, and transfer discrete units of data. It is the mechanism by which a machine records and accesses information, operating through fixed electronic circuits and binary code. It is static in nature, given that stored information remains exactly identical and at the same location. Neither time nor context alters it. Human memory operates according to an entirely different logic. In his account of the biology of memory, Nicholas Carr provides a historically grounded basis that debunks the metaphor of the brain working as a storage system. While computer memory is static and binary, biological memory is alive and unavoidably embodied. Citing neuroscientist Kobi Rosenblum, Carr explains that while a computer absorbs information and immediately saves it in fixed form, the human brain continues to process information long after it is received, and the quality of memories depends on how that information is processed over time. Unlike computational memory, which is immediate and every time identical to its input, memory consolidation is a slow, organic and multi-stage biological process. Short-term memories become long-term ones through complex biological processes of protein synthesis, growth of new synaptic terminals, and biochemical and anatomical changes at the cellular level. The quality of memories depends not on the quality of input but on how that information is processed across time, through sleep, dreams, pleasure, and trauma. Far from being a recollection of past events, memory is an active, organic mesh of different recollections and dispositions that consolidate into a set of representations always open to being re-signified. This biological understanding finds a psychic correlate in Freud. In Civilization and Its Discontents, opening with the famous analogy of Rome as a psychic space—a city in which every prior stage of construction coexists simultaneously with every subsequent layer, though transformed throughout time—Freud affirms that in the mind, unlike in physical space, “nothing that has once taken shape can be lost”, and that “the retention of all previous stages, together with the final shape, is possible only in the mind” (22). This does not mean that the human mind is not able to forget; rather, it argues that every lived experience persists in the psychic apparatus operating at varying levels of depth, reciprocally shaping and being re-shaped by the experiences that come after it. What persists in the mind does so dynamically, and appears transformed, repressed, distorted, only partially accessible, and always mediated by the ongoing psychic life of the subject. From a phenomenological perspective, this active memory is further elaborated by Ricoeur, for whom memory is an effortful practice of self-constitution. The self is the ongoing narrative it constructs across time—as opposed to the mechanical addition of the archive, the sum of what it has recorded. This narrative identity (what Ricoeur calls ipse) is constituted through the living act of remembering and interpreting, not stored within it; it is what ceases with death and cannot be archived. title: Working Memory as Programmable Fast Weight Computation
abstract: Abstract Working memory (WM) stores information after sensory input disappears and later retrieves it in a task-relevant format, but the mechanism unifying storage and retrieval remains unclear. Here we combine neural geometry analyses of macaque dorsolateral prefrontal cortex activity during a visuospatial delayed-match-to-sample task with computational modeling to test whether WM can be implemented as recurrent fast-weight computation. We found that the relational geometry of remembered locations was strongly expressed during sample presentation, degraded during the early delay, and reemerged before requirement in a partially distinct mnemonic subspace. A recurrent fast-weight programmer model, which implements a form of dynamic fast-weight memory closely related to linear Transformer computation, reproduced these latent-to-mnemonic dynamics. Direct inspection and perturbation of the model revealed that neural activity writes stimulus information into rapidly modifiable synaptic states, synaptic dynamics organize this latent memory over time, and recurrent readout queries the evolving state to generate task-relevant activity. These findings provide a unified account of WM storage and retrieval and suggest that biological WM and Transformer family architectures share an algorithmic principle of programmable temporary memory.

title: Flutter Boundary Prediction Based on Feature Extraction and Bayesian Optimization Transformer–Long Short-Term Memory
abstract: A data-driven approach for flutter boundary prediction is proposed, which adopts a deep learning model to extract flutter features from measured signals, thereby enabling the analysis of aeroelastic system stability. Following a modeling strategy that leverages structural acceleration response signals, a dataset is constructed from experimental data acquired from wind tunnel tests, and a multidimensional feature system and a set of comparative models are subsequently established for performance evaluation. Comparative analytical results reveal that the integration of power spectral density (PSD) with the Bayesian optimization Transformer–long short-term memory hybrid model can markedly enhance the efficacy of feature extraction and the accuracy of flutter boundary prediction. Experimental validation demonstrates that the proposed method achieves a mean prediction error of 3.73% for unseen working conditions of the wind tunnel model and 4.14% for data obtained from a single flight test sortie. Furthermore, a prediction error below 10% is achievable at approximately 70% of the critical flutter speed, which could contribute to enhanced early warning performance in flutter tests.

title: Gated Differentiable Working Memory for Long-Context Language Modeling
abstract: Long contexts break transformers: attention scores dilute across thousands of tokens, critical information gets lost in the middle, and the model cannot adapt to novel patterns at inference time. Recent work on test-time adaptation addresses this by maintaining a form of working memory---transient parameters updated on the current context---but existing approaches employ uniform write policies that waste computation on low-value regions and suffer from high gradient variance across semantically heterogeneous contexts. In this work, we reframe test-time adaptation as a budget-constrained memory consolidation problem, asking: given limited computational budget, which parts of the context should be consolidated into working memory? We propose GDWM (Gated Differentiable Working Memory), a framework that introduces a Write Controller to gate the memory consolidation process. Our controller estimates Contextual Utility---an information-theoretic measure quantifying how much each region depends on long-range context---and allocates gradient steps accordingly, subject to a coverage constraint that ensures global representation. Theoretically, we prove that our chunk-restricted sampling strategy reduces gradient variance by eliminating inter-chunk variance via the Law of Total Variance. Experiments on ZeroSCROLLS and LongBench v2 benchmarks demonstrate that GDWM achieves comparable or superior performance with 4 \times fewer gradient steps compared to uniform baselines---excelling on sparse-information tasks (+6--13% on Qasper, +5--13% on GovReport for smaller models) while revealing principled trade-offs on dense-coverage tasks, establishing a new efficiency-performance Pareto frontier for test-time adaptation.

title: From Cache to Cognition: Structural Parallels Between KV Cache Memory Management and Working Memory Constraints in LLM Inference
abstract: Key-Value (KV) cache memory consumption is a dominant bottleneck in long-context large language model (LLM) inference. For LLaMA-3.1 8B with batch size 10, KV cache memory grows from approximately 5 GB to 40 GB as sequence length increases from 1×10³ to 8×10³ tokens, eventually exceeding the fixed model-parameter footprint. This engineering pressure has driven a family of solutions—selective eviction, dynamic per-layer budget allocation, and latent-reasoning architectures—whose design logic structurally resembles principles from cognitive working memory research, even though the primary engineering literature does not invoke that framing. This paper identifies and defends three structural parallels: (1) per-layer dynamic cache budgeting in systems such as LAVa empirically requires differential memory allocation across transformer layers, analogous in structure (though not in mechanism) to the idea that different representational levels require different working-memory resources; (2) latent-reasoning architectures such as RiM explicitly invoke a working-memory analogy—decoupling internal computation from token externalization—though this analogy is asserted rather than empirically validated; and (3) hallucination in LLMs may be partially attributable to parametric compression constraints that force statistical generalization over rare facts. We frame these parallels as interpretive analogies grounded in engineering evidence, not as claims about shared mechanism, and identify what evidence would strengthen or refute each. Authorship: Saluca Agentic AI Research Team (Saluca LLC). AI-drafted from arXiv preprint corpus on the date in the filename. Cited arXiv preprints: 2605.30343v1
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: Memory efficiency and resource-rational encoding in sentence processing
abstract: There is a growing consensus that, in order to serve as models of human language processing, language models (LMs) need to be constrained in their use of memory for context, the analogue to human working memory (WM). Here we take a novel yet simple approach to constraining WM in language models, in a way that reflects models of human cognition where memory is treated as a limited resource and deployed strategically. In order to capture this constraint on memory encoding, we inject noise into the hidden representations of Transformer-based LMs at tunable rates. Then we train the models with a hybrid objective, such that they learn to maximize the performance of next-word prediction subject to explicit constraints on the total encoding precision. We find that explicit WM constraints improve the model's alignment with human reading times. More importantly, we find that the need to manage encoding precision reshapes the nature of the models' context representations, making them more compressed and categorical. Our results show how resource-rational models of WM allocation can be implemented in neural models simply and successfully, and point to a dissociation between WM retrieval mechanisms and the underlying memory representations in models of human sentence processing.

title: Reinforcement learning-driven adaptive game therapy for cognitive impairment patients with improved vision transformer based detection model
abstract: BACKGROUND: Cognitive impairment is the growing challenge that requires early diagnosis and personalized management of neurodegenerative conditions like Alzheimer's disease. Neuroimaging modalities like Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) provide valuable structural and functional insights into brain changes associated with cognitive decline. However, existing deep learning (DL) based diagnostic models have the challenges in non-consideration of long-range spatial dependencies and contextual information across brain slices that lead to suboptimal classification accuracy. METHODS: To overcome the limitations, this research introduces the framework that combines an Improved Vision Transformer (Im-ViT) with the Residual Simple Recurrent Unit (ResNet-SRU) based Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) to capture spatial and temporal dependencies in neuroimaging data. Preprocessing using Multiscale Gaussian Filter (MGF) enhances feature clarity by removing multiscale noise. In addition, the system integrates the Visual Working Memory (VWM)-based game therapy, where difficulty levels dynamically adapt using the proposed Iterative Hiking-based Reinforcement Learning (ItHRL) approach. RESULTS: The analysis of the proposed model based on various assessment measures like Accuracy, Recall, Precision, F-Score, Specificity, and Mean Squared Error (MSE) acquired the values of 99.62%, 99.33%, 98.97%, 99.56%, 99.62% and 0.018 respectively. CONCLUSIONS: The proposed model with combined detection and game therapy approach yield higher classification accuracy, faster convergence and patient engagement.

title: Decoupling Knowledge and Reasoning: A Brain-Inspired Architecture for Traceable, Hallucination-Free AI with Quantified Uncertainty — Implementation Report
abstract: Prototype implementation of a brain-inspired three-module AI architecture (Hippocampus, Working Memory, Neocortex). Implements hierarchical predictive coding with energy-based inference-time optimization, three-layer knowledge storage (FAISS + Sentence-Transformers), uncertainty propagation, soft-stop mechanism, and hallucination-free KNN decoder. Reports training results, structural dependency experiment (severed hippocampal input → architectural abort), decoder results, and representation leakage test. Companion to conceptual paper DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.20683132.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: A novel cross-domain invention generation framework
abstract: Artificial intelligence has achieved strong performance in pattern recognition and decision automation, yet its ability to support improvised innovation and deliberate invention remains limited. Most contemporary systems operate in a procedural or “autopilot” mode, recombining previously learned patterns without the conscious-like control required for goal-directed synthesis across unfamiliar domains. In this work, we introduce a cognitively inspired and mathematically grounded framework that formalizes invention as cross-domain symbolic transfer, augmented by an explicit workingmemory system that enables deliberate reasoning, structural alignment, and controlled synthesis beyond procedural generation. The proposed architecture separates procedural intelligence, provided by pretrained foundation models, from consciouslike inventive reasoning implemented through a working-memory system composed of semantic memory, episodic memory, transformer-based state construction, and a multi-agent reinforcement learning controller. Episodic memory stores validated reasoning trajectories and reusable invention tokens, while a working-memory–inspired control process orchestrates multi-step reasoning episodes that align latent symbolic representations across domains. Invention is cast as a constrained, experience-driven search process in which multiple policy networks explore alternative reasoning actions under feedback from an environmental model. Graph-structured episodic memory and graph embeddings are used to encode and retrieve prior reasoning episodes, enabling cumulative experience accumulation and transfer across tasks. Retrieval-augmented reasoning further extends semantic memory with relevant external knowledge from databases and domain-specific repositories. To ensure trustworthy generative behavior, the framework incorporates an assurance layer that evaluates candidate inventions for utility, novelty, feasibility, and parsimony against invalid cross-domain mappings. Successful reasoning trajectories and validated invention outcomes are consolidated into episodic memory, enabling continual improvement over time. By integrating conscious-like working-memory mechanisms, analogy-driven synthesis, reinforcement learning, and graph-structured episodic experience, this framework advances generative AI from procedural pattern reproduction toward accountable, interpretable, and trustworthy invention across different domains.

title: AuraMind Technical Brief: Engineering Detail of the Emotion-Modulated Quantum-Assisted Neural Architecture
abstract: A technical brief providing quantitative engineering detail of the AuraMind Emotion-Modulated Quantum-Assisted Neural Architecture. Written for peer scientists, engineers, and research groups working in adjacent areas (cognitive architectures, hybrid neural systems, persistent memory for AI agents, affective computing, hybrid classical-quantum machine learning, neuromorphic deployment of large models) who want a focused technical overview of the architecture. Topics include the hybrid neural backbone composition (state-space and transformer hybrids), Emotion Control Vector (ECV) specification, multi-modal memory schema (episodic, semantic, procedural, affective), reasoning engine modules, quantum-assisted subroutines for combinatorial planning, safety supervisor architecture, seven-stage training pipeline, and six-stage inference pipeline with test-time compute scaling. The work is conducted independently and shared in alignment with NASA Transform to Open Science (TOPS) initiative. Keywords: AuraMind; hybrid neural architectures; Emotion Control Vector; persistent memory; quantum-assisted machine learning; cognitive architectures; technical brief; independent research.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: The Stateful Attention Unit
abstract: Current AI architectures---from RNNs to Transformers---share a limitation: their internal state either decays exponentially (LSTM) or resets entirely after each forward pass (Transformer). We propose the Stateful Attention Unit (SAU), a computational building block that maintains a persistent state vector across calls, updating it incrementally via cross-attention between state and input. Stacking SAU blocks into a three-layer network with distinct time scales (perception, working memory, and core state), we introduce a slow-channel consolidation mechanism that accumulates surprise signals and periodically injects them into the core. The system also supports an idle mode where internal states evolve without external input. At 268K parameters on synthetic data, we observe four properties: (1) familiarity detection without training, (2) time-scale separation between layers, (3) slow-channel consolidation at calibrated thresholds, and (4) self-driven idle state dynamics. These are small-scale prototype observations, not claims of production capability. We open-source the implementation as a platform for studying persistent-state architectures.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: Planning-aligned Token Compression for Long-Context Autonomous Driving
abstract: Monolithic vision-action models represent an emerging paradigm in autonomous driving. However, this architecture produces token sequences that quickly exceed real-time computational budgets when encoding extended temporal context for complex interactions. While approaches like linear transformers and external memory try to make the context lightweight, token compression is most compatible with the architecture as it requires no backbone modifications. Yet existing compression adopts rule-based heuristics like temporal decay, decoupled from planning, risking loss of decision-critical information. We propose COMPACT-VA, a planning-aligned working memory framework built on conditional VQ-VAE, compressing extended context into bounded representations. Compression is conditioned on both historical trajectory and a learned planning intent that the posterior encoder distills from future trajectories during training, while the prior encoder learns to predict it from compressed observations. The compressed memory, concatenated with the predicted latent, feeds the policy for end-to-end optimization, planning with retained decision-critical information. We evaluate on high-signal dynamic scenarios where historical context is most critical for behavior correctness (e.g., stop, yield, or proceed), and accordingly design behavioral metrics. Under comparable token budgets, we achieve >6% improvement (68.3%) on success rates with consistent gains across metrics. Ablations validate planning-aligned coupling effectiveness. Closed-loop evaluation confirms that COMPACT-VA maintained general driving performance with 3.3* speedup and 2.7* memory reduction over uncompressed processing.

title: Hierarchical Global Attention (HGA)
abstract: Hierarchical Global Attention (HGA) is a drop-in replacement for dense causal attention in pretrained long-context transformers. HGA preserves the original checkpoint parameters: the pretrained W_Q, W_K, W_V, and W_O projections remain unchanged, no calibration parameters are introduced, and no retraining is required. Applied to Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507-FP8 on a single RTX~5090 (32GB), the patched model runs out of the box at a 64K-token context, where token-level K/V storage is not feasible on this hardware. Unlike previous sparse-attention methods, HGA performs hierarchical two-level routing. It first retrieves relevant chunks using compact RoPE-aware summaries and then refines the selection by routing only the most relevant groups before performing exact token-level attention. This hierarchical retrieval significantly reduces the number of fetched tokens while preserving exact attention over the retrieved token set, making RAM- and NVMe-backed storage practical. The full historical token K/V resides in host RAM or NVMe storage, while only a small routed working set is transferred to GPU memory during attention. Consequently, GPU memory consumption depends primarily on model weights and the routed working set rather than on the total context length. Across all tested context lengths (4K - 64K tokens), routed attention remains within approximately 0.01--0.02 nats of dense attention while the sparsity used is just about 3%. These results suggest that the approximation introduced by hierarchical routing is small, and that the remaining quality gap is likely dominated by long-context positional encoding rather than by the routing algorithm itself.

title: APUT: Large Language Models as Cross-Modal Consistency Reasoning Engines for Egocentric State Estimation
abstract: Current multimodal large language models (LLMs) excel at passive representation alignment. However, in highly dynamic, partially observable environments (e.g., egocentric vision with severe occlusion and the “cocktail party” effect), standard models suffer from representational collapse. Unobserved targets are frequently dropped from working memory or their states are hallucinated. To address this, the Active-Perception Unified Transformer (APUT) is proposed. Crucially, APUT is not designed as an improved multimodal tracker, but rather as a reasoning-based state estimator. Identity tracking is treated as a dynamic constraint satisfaction problem (CSP). By modeling a structured state matrix through a dedicated encoder, the LLM operates over explicit tokenized world states. Implicit latent tracking collapses under contradictory cross-modal evidence because state representations are entangled, whereas explicit constraint graphs allow for discrete hypothesis elimination. Furthermore, a partial delta-update mechanism and a multiphase training pipeline, ranging from teacher-forced alignment to critic-guided hypothesis ranking, are introduced. Through this architecture, it is demonstrated how robust object permanence emerges from internal logical coherence under supervised structured learning, providing a novel paradigm for embodied state estimation.
venue: Journal of Frontiers in Technology and Engineering Integration

title: Maximum Intelligence Is Not Maximum Output. Maximum Intelligence Is Maximum Useful Cognition Per Token.
abstract: Tokenomics as a Cognitive Resource Allocation Framework for Efficient AI Systems Abstract Modern AI systems increasingly depend on large context windows, expensive inference, and repeated token generation to perform reasoning, planning, and communication. However, token usage is usually treated as a passive cost of language production rather than as an active control variable. This paper introduces Tokenomics: a cognitive resource allocation framework for AI systems that treats tokens as scarce units of compute, attention, memory bandwidth, and decision surface. The central thesis is that intelligent systems should optimize not for maximum token output, but for maximum cognitive value per token. Tokenomics proposes that useful intelligence emerges not only from model scale, but from disciplined allocation of tokens toward salience, compression, retrieval, reasoning, action, and consolidation. The framework connects information theory, adaptive computation, sparse activation, retrieval-augmented generation, agent reflection, and practical operating-system design. It argues that “knowledge infinity between tokens” is not literal infinity, but a design principle: each emitted token should compress a deeper internal model, enabling short outputs to carry high decision density. The paper proposes an architecture for Tokenomic AI Systems built around salience gating, sparse module recruitment, context budgeting, memory compression, response arbitration, red-team checking, and post-task consolidation. Keywords tokenomics, AI systems, inference efficiency, cognitive compression, sparse activation, adaptive computation, salience, agent architecture, retrieval-augmented generation, cognitive operating systems Introduction AI systems currently face a paradox. Larger models and longer contexts increase capability, yet every additional token carries inference cost, latency, attention burden, and user cognitive load. In practical use, more tokens do not automatically produce more intelligence. A long response may be shallow, while a short response may contain dense strategy, compressed reasoning, and operational leverage. This paper proposes Tokenomics as a formal operating doctrine for AI systems. In this context, a token is not merely a text fragment. It is a unit of compute expenditure, attention allocation, memory surface, and decision exposure. Tokenomics asks: how should an intelligent system spend tokens the way a disciplined organization spends capital? The answer is not simply “use fewer tokens.” The goal is to use fewer wasted tokens and more high-yield tokens. A high-yield token contributes to one or more of the following: accurate decision-making compressed knowledge transfer useful action risk reduction memory consolidation future reuse system-level learning This reframes AI output generation as a resource-governance problem. The system must decide where to spend tokens, when to compress, when to expand, when to retrieve, when to reason, and when to stop. Tokenomic Measurement System v1 1. Bad tokens: restate obvious context sound smart but do not change action add structure without leverage expand when the user needs execution hide uncertainty under clean language 2. Cognitive return can be scored across five buckets: CR=DecisionQuality+Actionability+RiskControl+ReuseValue+LearningGainCR = DecisionQuality + Actionability + RiskControl + ReuseValue + LearningGainCR=DecisionQuality+Actionability+RiskControl+ReuseValue+LearningGain For your systems, score each 0–5: Metric Question Decision Quality Did the answer improve the actual decision? Salience Allocation Equations Before generating, the system ranks what deserves token budget. Si=αUi+βRi+γMi+δTi+ϵNi−ζKiS_i = \alpha U_i + \beta R_i + \gamma M_i + \delta T_i + \epsilon N_i - \zeta K_iSi=αUi+βRi+γMi+δTi+ϵNi−ζKi Where: UiU_iUi = urgency RiR_iRi = risk / consequence MiM_iMi = mission relevance TiT_iTi = time sensitivity NiN_iNi = novelty / uncertainty KiK_iKi = known / already-settled context Plain version: Spend tokens on what is urgent, risky, mission-relevant, time-sensitive, uncertain, and not already known. Then allocate output budget: Bi=Btotal⋅Si∑SB_i = B_{total} \cdot \frac{S_i}{\sum S}Bi=Btotal⋅∑SSi Meaning each topic only gets tokens proportional to its salience. This prevents the system from overexplaining low-value context. 4. Compression Efficiency Metrics Compression is not just shorter. It must preserve meaning. CE=MeaningPreservedTokensUsedCE = \frac{MeaningPreserved}{TokensUsed}CE=TokensUsedMeaningPreserved A stronger version: CEF=InformationRetained+ActionClarity+RiskPreservedOutputTokensCEF = \frac{InformationRetained + ActionClarity + RiskPreserved}{OutputTokens}CEF=OutputTokensInformationRetained+ActionClarity+RiskPreserved Good compression: fewer words same or better decision quality risks still visible next move clearer reusable rule extracted Bad compression: short but vague hides uncertainty loses tradeoffs sounds confident without basis So every compressed output should pass: Can the user still act correctly?If yes, compression worked.If no, it was just deletion. 5. Benchmark Tasks To prove Tokenomics works, compare two systems: System A: Non-tokenomic Normal verbose AI response. System B: Tokenomic Uses salience, compression, token budget, risk control, and reusable-rule extraction. Benchmark across task classes: Task Type Example Invoice task Update invoice, rebalance math, produce PDF Estimating task Price a furniture install from messy scope Cashflow task Decide whether to schedule crew before payment Research task Turn doctrine into paper section Architecture task Design AI runtime module Red-team task Find failure modes in plan Memory task Convert repeated pattern into reusable rule Score each output on: Score=DQ+ACT+RISK+REUSE+ACCURACY−WASTEScore = DQ + ACT + RISK + REUSE + ACCURACY - WASTEScore=DQ+ACT+RISK+REUSE+ACCURACY−WASTE Then compare: TokenomicGain=ScoreBTokensB−ScoreATokensATokenomicGain = \frac{Score_B}{Tokens_B} - \frac{Score_A}{Tokens_A}TokenomicGain=TokensBScoreB−TokensAScoreA If System B gives equal or better score with fewer tokens, Tokenomics is working. Implementation Architecture 1. Runtime loop Classify task Rank salience Set token budget Recruit only needed agents Generate deep internal model Compress surface output Check risk preservation Score cognitive return Consolidate reusable rule The key is this: Reasoning can be deep internally, but expression must be economically govern 2. Background 2.1 Information and Compression Information theory established that communication can be analyzed in terms of information, uncertainty, redundancy, and efficient encoding [1]. Tokenomics inherits this view but applies it to AI reasoning and interaction. The system should minimize low-value redundancy while preserving decision-critical information. In human terms, good communication is not always shorter; it is better compressed. Compression does not mean deleting meaning. It means removing waste while preserving structure. 2.2 Transformers and Token-Centric Computation Transformer models process sequences through attention mechanisms, making tokens central to both computation and context management [2]. In these systems, token count affects not only output length but also memory use, latency, and attention complexity. Tokenomics treats this as an architectural fact: token flow is compute flow. 2.3 Scaling Laws and Compute-Aware Training Scaling-law research shows that model capability depends on the relationship between model size, data, and compute [3]. Later inference-aware work argues that deployment cost must also be considered, not just training cost [4]. Tokenomics extends this reasoning from model development into runtime behavior: the system should optimize inference output for value, not volume. 2.4 Adaptive Computation Adaptive Computation Time allows neural networks to vary computation depending on problem difficulty [5]. Tokenomics applies a similar principle to response generation and agent operation: simple tasks should receive sparse, direct output, while complex tasks should receive deeper reasoning and structured synthesis. 2.5 Sparse Activation and Mixture-of-Experts Sparse expert models demonstrate that not every parameter or expert must activate for every input. Switch Transformers and related MoE systems show that sparse routing can increase scale while limiting active computation [6]. title: Constrained-Execution Agentic Analytics for Regulated Data: An Architecture Pattern for Trustworthy LLM Cohort Analytics, with a Reproducibility Case Study (Deterministic Dispatch: 33% → 100%)
abstract: Large language model agents are increasingly used for analytics over regulated healthcare claims data, yet the common designs — a single tool-using "super agent", or a free-form crew of agents that writes and runs code — are hard to reproduce, audit, and trust. We present Claim-FM, a working prototype for healthcare claims analytics in which language models are used for planning and interpretation while every data operation is executed through a constrained set of typed, deterministic primitives: the models reason, and the primitives compute. A crew of four agents (Planner, Analyst, Critic, Responder) is driven by a runtime that owns the shape of the pipeline; the agents do not call each other, and no model ever produces a reported number — a model decides what to run and explains the result, while typed primitives compute every value. We report four empirical results. (1) Deterministic dispatch — replacing free-form hand-off with a fixed runtime path — raises multi-step plan reliability from 33% to 100% on a synthetic benchmark at no additional cost; the effect is at the architecture level, not the model level. (2) A critic that runs adversarially only on high-stakes intents (about 30% of queries) bounds the trust-versus-latency cost. (3) A training-shaped audit log makes every run replayable and directly usable as fine-tuning data; fine-tuning the Planner (Qwen3-4B with LoRA) on this audit-shaped corpus moves a 195-case planner benchmark from 1.8 to 91.6. (4) A transferable deployment failure: the fine-tuned model silently lost accuracy in production when it was served a prompt that differed structurally from the one used to score it, with symptoms that imitated a hardware out-of-memory error and a flaky model; a replay audit over 70 conversations and 136 turns confirmed that the fix held within a fixed configuration (0 OOM; 91.2% raw success). The contributions are the constrained-execution pattern, described openly enough to reproduce; the measured architecture-level reliability result; the training-shaped audit method and the fine-tune it produced; and the prompt-contract failure mode together with the replay method used to diagnose it. Scope is stated plainly: the evaluation uses a synthetic demonstrator of about 2,300 patients, and the separate claims foundation model (a masked-event embeddings transformer) is left untrained. Concurrent commercial systems are cited as prior art, not as head-to-head comparisons. This Zenodo record is the canonical, citable version of record for this work.

title: An Adaptive Medical Virtual Simulation Training System Based on Deep Reinforcement Learning: Multi-modal Learner Modelling and Empirical Evaluation of Pedagogical Effectiveness
- Inggeris: Alternative View: Resources, Civilization Cycles and the Path Forward
abstract: 📘 ALTERNATIVE VIEW: RESOURCES, CIVILIZATION CYCLES AND THE PATH FORWARD Author: M. Ishak bin OsmanDate: 25 June 2026License: Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0)Statement: This is a personal perspective based on established facts, logic, observation and personal experience. The section regarding the possibility of earlier advanced civilizations is a logical hypothesis and reflection only, not a scientifically proven fact. Based on scientific research and global energy data, the main reserves of resources on Earth are finite and decrease year by year. Official estimates state: - Natural gas: Approximately 60 to 90 years remaining at current consumption rates.- Crude oil and petroleum: Approximately 60 to 120 years remaining; conservative estimates often cite 50 to 80 years, while accounting for improved extraction technology and new reserves, this may extend to around 100–120 years.- Strategic metals and minerals: Approximately 70 to 200 years remaining. These are not mere assumptions; this data is recorded and updated annually by international energy agencies, and can be verified by anyone through official reports and public sources. Oil is not only fuel for vehicles — it is used to generate electricity, acts as a coolant and insulator in electrical equipment, lubricant for all types of machinery, and serves as the base material for plastics, rubber, fertilizers, and medicines. It cannot be regenerated quickly; its formation takes 50 to 100 million years from the remains of ancient organisms, buried, compressed, and heated deep within the Earth. ⚡ WHAT HAPPENS WHEN OIL RUNS OUT COMPLETELY? This is a critical question: if all oil in the world is exhausted, and even the remaining stock used for electricity systems, transformers, and lubricants becomes scarce, what will logically happen? We can break it down step by step: ✅ Phase 1: Economic and social adjustmentBefore reaching total collapse, the first noticeable effects appear in daily life. Unemployment rises sharply, as most industries, transport, and services depend entirely on oil‑based energy and materials. Businesses reduce operations or close down, causing economic activity to slow and eventually stop. The banking system can no longer function normally; banks are forced to close, and the value of paper money loses its meaning as trade and production come to a halt. Prices of essential goods increase rapidly due to limited supply and higher production costs. ✅ Phase 2: When insulating and lubricating oil also run outThis is the turning point: - Without insulating oil, transformers and high‑voltage equipment will overheat, fail, and cannot be repaired or replaced — there is no substitute that works as well or in sufficient quantity.- Without lubricants, all engines, turbines, and moving parts will grind to a halt; metal surfaces will overheat, wear out, and seize up.- We may try alternatives such as vegetable oils or animal fats, but these are not suitable for high‑voltage use, do not last long, and are available only in very limited amounts. ✅ Phase 3: The chain of industry breaksEven though we can still use hydro, wind, and solar energy to generate electricity, this alone is not enough to sustain modern civilization: - These sources can produce power, but they cannot melt iron, make glass, create new transformers, or manufacture complex machinery — all of which require high heat, precise processes, and a full industrial supply chain.- Once existing equipment breaks down, no new parts or replacements can be made. Factories will shut down permanently because you need energy and machines to build new machines — a cycle that cannot be restarted once the key fuel is gone. ✅ Final outcomeWhen oil is completely exhausted, the entire industrial system collapses gradually. Electricity grids fail, production stops, and we lose the ability to maintain modern infrastructure. Knowledge and skills remain in memory, but there is no way to apply them without the necessary materials and energy. Inevitably, humanity returns to a simpler way of life, relying directly on nature, wood, water, and fire — just as our ancestors did long ago. ⚡ WHY IT IS DIFFICULT TO REPLACE OIL USING EARTH’S RESOURCES ALONE Many ask: Why not simply find alternatives on Earth instead of travelling far into space? The answer is clear based on facts: While we can use hydro, wind, solar, or nuclear energy, all have limits. These sources can generate electricity, but they cannot fully replace oil’s functions as a high‑density fuel, lubricant, insulator, and raw material for thousands of industrial products. Nuclear fuel also exists on Earth, but its reserves are limited as well. If used on a large scale to replace all oil demand, it too would be exhausted within a relatively short time. The conclusion: There is no other resource on Earth abundant and long‑lasting enough to sustain our civilization at its current level. Even if alternatives exist, their quantity is insufficient for the long term. We must also understand that having energy alone is not enough. For example, a water wheel can produce power, but it cannot melt iron, make glass, or manufacture complex machinery. If the wheel breaks, we cannot easily replace its parts — because making new parts requires factories, tools, and high heat, all of which depend on the same supply chain and energy sources. Even a simple light bulb cannot be made by hand or using only fire; it requires specialized materials, high temperatures, and precise processes that only industrial systems can provide. Once those systems stop, no more bulbs or replacement parts can be produced. 🚀 THE TRUE PURPOSE OF EXPLORING SPACE Thus, travelling to the Moon, Mars, or other destinations is not merely empty exploration or a desire to conquer new worlds. The goal is clear and essential: ✅ NOT to find oil or gas as on EarthIt must be understood: Oil and natural gas do not exist elsewhere. They form only through a unique process requiring millions of years of organic remains and specific environmental conditions — conditions that have never existed on the Moon or Mars. ✅ TO FIND RAW MATERIALS FOR NEW ENERGY SOURCESAlthough there is no oil, other valuable resources can be found and processed: - Ice and frozen water: Found in large quantities at Mars’ poles and beneath the lunar surface. It can be split into hydrogen and oxygen — the most powerful rocket propellant, while also providing breathable oxygen and water for daily use.- Materials for nuclear energy: The Moon contains Helium‑3, ideal for fusion energy — a powerful, clean, and long‑lasting energy source. Mars holds natural radioactive elements such as uranium and thorium, usable to power nuclear reactors.- Gases and minerals: Mars’ atmosphere is rich in carbon dioxide, which can be processed into various essential materials. Rocks on both worlds contain iron, aluminium, silicon, and other elements for construction. The main objective is to develop a new energy system that no longer depends entirely on Earth’s fossil reserves. If we master extracting and processing off‑world resources, we can operate there while reducing the strain on our home planet. 🔭 SEARCHING FOR SIGNS OF LIFE BEYOND EARTH Another area of research is looking for signs of life and habitable environments elsewhere. Space agencies use telescopes and specialized instruments to study planets and stars. Officially, this research aims to deepen our understanding of life’s origins, the formation of the universe, and whether life exists beyond Earth. If a more advanced civilization is discovered, it could open opportunities to learn new knowledge and technology to help solve our challenges. 🤖 ABOUT ROBOTS: THEIR LIMITATIONS AND TIME REQUIRED It is true that humans build increasingly advanced robots. However, progress happens in stages, not instantly. It takes a long time to develop fully autonomous, self‑sufficient systems. For the near future, robots have clear limitations:✅ Still require human guidance and controlWhile programmable for specific tasks, robots lack independent thinking, decision‑making, or problem‑solving for unforeseen situations. If an obstacle, malfunction, or environmental change occurs, they stop working until instructed. ✅ Remote control is severely limitedLong distances create signal delays. Sending a command from Earth to Mars takes 4 to 24 minutes, and the response takes equally long. This means no real‑time control. Tasks requiring precision and speed become slow, risky, and difficult to complete. ✅ Cannot build large‑scale systems independentlyEven if robots are sent first, they cannot construct stations, process resources, or establish full facilities without direct human presence and oversight. Their role is limited to initial simple work, not long‑term infrastructure. Conclusion:One day, fully capable robots may exist, but that requires far more time than we currently have. In the near term, robots are only assistants, not replacements. Without humans or highly advanced control systems, they cannot complete major tasks effectively. This is another reason why this effort is time‑consuming and difficult to finish before Earth’s main resources begin to decline. ⚠️ CHALLENGES AHEAD To date, we have not successfully established permanent human settlements on other planets, and the journey faces great difficulties: - Distance and travel time: The closest approach to Mars is 55–60 million km, taking 6–9 months one way. A round trip may take 2–3 years. During this time, humans are exposed to harmful cosmic radiation without Earth’s protective atmosphere.- Technical hurdles: Landing safely on Mars is difficult due to its thin atmosphere. Providing enough supplies and living conditions is even harder.- No existing infrastructure: There is no shelter, breathable air, clean water, or mild temperatures — temperatures can drop below -60°C.
